reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: Results from prolonged immersion of the feet in water, causing maceration and injury of the skin and underlying soft tissue
Warm water immersion foot causes painful, white, wrinkled, macerated soles after prolonged exposure, while cold water forms overlap with non-freezing cold injury (trench foot)
The prolonged damp exposure and skin barrier breakdown predispose to secondary bacterial and fungal infection
The feet are typically tender, swollen, and blanched or wrinkled, with discomfort on walking
Management is drying the feet thoroughly, rest, elevation, and allowing the skin to recover, with treatment of any secondary infection
Keeping feet dry, changing wet socks and footwear frequently, and airing the feet are the cornerstones of prevention
Warm water immersion foot generally recovers quickly once the feet are kept dry, unlike the more prolonged course of cold non-freezing injury
reference.pathophysiology: Immersion foot develops when the feet are kept wet for prolonged periods, leading to maceration of the epidermis, disruption of the skin barrier, and softening of the horny layer. In warm water exposure the predominant problem is skin breakdown, oedema, and secondary infection, whereas prolonged cold wet exposure adds cold-induced vasoconstriction and microvascular injury that overlaps with trench foot. The waterlogged, damaged skin loses its protective function, causing pain, swelling, and susceptibility to bacterial and fungal invasion.
additionalDifferentials: Tinea pedis and other fungal skin infection
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from history of prolonged water exposure and characteristic macerated feet
Examination for maceration, blistering, secondary infection, and neurovascular status
Skin swabs or scrapings if bacterial or fungal infection is suspected
Inflammatory markers where cellulitis or systemic infection is a concern
Assessment for coexisting cold injury when exposure was in cold water
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, abscess, or systemic signs of infection
Features of coexisting freezing injury after cold exposure
reference.prognosis: Warm water immersion foot usually resolves within days once the feet are dried and rested; the main complication is secondary infection, while cold water forms overlapping with non-freezing cold injury can have a more protracted recovery.
pitfalls: Failing to keep the feet dry, allowing the injury to persist or worsen
Missing secondary bacterial or fungal infection
Not distinguishing warm from cold water forms, which differ in course and management
Overlooking preventive foot care in those with ongoing wet exposure
management: Remove the feet from the wet environment and thoroughly dry, warm and rest them to allow the macerated skin barrier to recover
Elevate the limb to reduce oedema and provide analgesia for pain, which may be neuropathic in the cold-water (non-freezing cold injury) form
Treat secondary bacterial infection with antistaphylococcal and antistreptococcal antibiotics, and use topical antifungal agents for superimposed dermatophyte or candidal infection
Meticulous wound care with regular inspection for blistering, cellulitis and tissue breakdown
Prevent recurrence by keeping the feet dry, changing wet socks and footwear frequently and airing the feet
Assess for and manage coexisting cold injury when exposure was in cold water, using gradual rewarming rather than rapid heat
